narrative:
The model estimates a 90% chance that you will leave your job. In practical terms, this is a very strong flight-risk signal: unless conditions change, the model expects you to move on, so the organization has treated the promotion decision as high-risk rather than assuming you will stay and grow.

The strongest reason is your total career experience. Being in the 6–10 year range stood out as the largest push toward leaving; compared with the most common staying group, which has 1–5 years, your broader experience makes you more mobile. The second factor is that you have received other job opportunities. This was a strong leaving signal and is relatively uncommon among employees predicted to stay, suggesting outside options are influencing the forecast. Third, your time in the current organization, in the 1–5 year range, also added to the leaving risk, even though that tenure length is common among stayers.

Before revisiting promotion, the organization should discuss your career path, pay and recognition, and whether a promotion would genuinely improve retention. You should clarify what would keep you engaged; if the answer is limited, a development or retention plan with a clear review point is more appropriate than denying promotion solely on a forecast.
